title: The Search for Truth
subtitle: Spiritual Seclusion, the Hunafa', and the Cave of Hira
summary: The spiritual crisis of pre-Islamic Makkah, the isolated monotheistic seekers known as the Hunafa', the encounter with Zayd ibn 'Amr, Muhammad's growing love for solitude and contemplative devotion (tahannuth), his retreats to the Cave of Hira atop Jabal al-Nur, and the truthful dreams that heralded divine revelation.

sections.text: The Religious Crisis of Pre-Islamic Makkah

As Muhammad ﷺ approached his late thirties, the stark moral and spiritual contradictions of Makkan society weighed heavily upon his reflective spirit. The city was flourishing economically, but ethically and religiously it languished in profound confusion. The Kaaba, originally consecrated by the Prophet Ibrahim as the earth's first sanctuary for the uncompromised worship of the One God, had been surrounded by three hundred and sixty stone idols, each representing tribal superstitions and fabricated intercessors.

Beyond stone worship, the social fabric was scarred by deeply rooted injustices: female infanticide (wa'd al-banat), in which infant daughters were buried alive out of dread of economic poverty or perceived tribal disgrace; aggressive usury that plunged debtors into hereditary servitude; and reckless clan feuds that consumed generations over minor insults. To an observant heart attuned to innate righteousness, the spiritual sterility of pagan polytheism offered neither moral guidance nor genuine solace.

Muhammad was not alone in his rejection of idolatry. A small, scattered group of Makkans, known in classical history as the Hunafa' (singular: Hanif, those who inclined to the pure faith), had rejected polytheism and sought the religion of Ibrahim. Ibn Ishaq relates that during one of Quraysh's festivals at an idol, four men withdrew from the crowds and met privately: Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, 'Uthman ibn al-Huwayrith, and 'Ubaydullah ibn Jahsh.

They said to one another, in Ibn Ishaq's account: 'By God, you know that your people are upon nothing; they worship a stone that neither hears nor sees nor harms nor benefits. Seek a religion for yourselves.' Waraqah turned to Christianity and its scriptures, while Zayd ibn 'Amr kept to a solitary monotheism. Sahih al-Bukhari records that he criticized Quraysh for slaughtering animals in the names of idols, and that he would take in baby girls whose fathers meant to bury them, raising them at his own expense.

Sahih al-Bukhari also relates that Muhammad met Zayd ibn 'Amr in the lower part of the valley of Baldah before revelation came to him. A dish of meat was offered to the Prophet and he declined to eat from it. Zayd then said: 'I do not eat of what you slaughter upon your stone altars, and I eat only that over which the name of God has been mentioned.' Zayd died before the prophethood began.
The rugged crags and silent heights of Mount Hira rising above the desert basin.
The Love for Solitude and Contemplation

In the narration of 'A'ishah recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, the prelude to divine guidance began when an intense love for solitude (khalwah) was instilled into Muhammad's heart. He withdrew from the noisy commercial clamor, festive poetry contests, and idolatrous rituals of Makkah, feeling drawn to contemplative prayer under the vast open expanse of the desert sky.

He chose for his retreats a small cave near the top of a mountain north-east of Makkah, known later as Jabal al-Nur (the Mountain of Light). Known as the Cave of Hira, it is reached by a steep climb over rough rock. It is commonly said that from its mouth one can see towards the sanctuary of the Kaaba.
The Practice of Tahannuth in Cave Hira

In the narration of 'A'ishah in Sahih al-Bukhari, he would spend a number of nights in the cave in devotion (tahannuth) before returning to his family, taking provisions with him for the stay. Ibn Ishaq relates that he made this retreat for a month each year, in Ramadan.
In the same narration, when his provisions ran out he would return to Khadijah and take provisions for a similar stay, until the truth came to him while he was in the Cave of Hira.
The starry desert night sky over the Hijaz mountains, witness to long nights of contemplative prayer.
The Herald of Revelation: True Dreams

Before the revelation itself, it began in the form of true dreams (al-ru'ya al-sadiqah). 'A'ishah relates in Sahih al-Bukhari that the first form of revelation to the Messenger of God ﷺ was good dreams in his sleep, and that every dream he saw came to pass like the breaking of dawn. Some scholars estimated that this period lasted about six months.

"The commencement of the divine inspiration to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in the form of true dreams during sleep. He never saw a dream except that it came true like the bright gleam of dawn." — Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 3; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 160

These luminous visions prepared his human faculties for the monumental spiritual weight of divine revelation. As the forty-year mark approached in the quiet month of Ramadan, the solitary seeker in Cave Hira stood at the threshold of world history. The long centuries of spiritual silence were about to be shattered by the eternal speech of the Creator.
